KPMG in Romania and Moldova: Local Talent, Regional Impact and New Leaders on the Team Finance People News Latest News Published on October 1, 2026 By Magda Purice Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email The contribution of KPMG leaders from Romania and Moldova is being recognized both locally and regionally through the assumption of new responsibilities within KPMG’s Central and Eastern Europe leadership team. Ramona Jurubiță takes on the role of Head of Clients & Markets for Central and Eastern Europe, while continuing in parallel her mandate as Country Managing Partner of KPMG in Romania and Moldova. René Schöb is appointed Head of Tax & Legal for KPMG in Central and Eastern Europe, while Mădălina Racovițan, Tax Partner and Head of People Services, takes on the role of Head of Tax & Legal for KPMG in Romania and Moldova. KPMG in Romania and Moldova is further strengthening its leadership team with the appointment of Raluca Enache and Alexandru Chirigiu as Partners, as well as a series of promotions to Associate Partner, Director, Senior Manager, Manager and other key positions across the organization. These appointments and promotions reflect the firm’s continued commitment to supporting professional development, recognizing the achievements of those who contribute to the organization’s success, and developing the next generation of leaders. Raluca Enache, Tax Partner, Head of EU Tax Centre Raluca has joined the KPMG Partnership in Romania and Moldova, while continuing in her role as leader of KPMG’s EU Tax Centre group for the EMA (Europe, Middle East and Africa) region. With more than 19 years of experience, Raluca supports clients and KPMG member firms in understanding the complexities of European tax law and assessing the impact of European and international tax developments on their operations across Europe. She coordinates KPMG’s network of European Union tax law specialists and analyzes how EU Member States implement key EU and OECD initiatives. Raluca frequently represents KPMG in its engagement with European institutions, with a focus on anti-abuse measures and tax transparency initiatives, and is a member of the leadership group coordinating KPMG’s global network of international tax and M&A tax specialists. Alexandru Chirigiu, Tax Partner, Head of Accounting & Tax Compliance Alexandru joins KPMG’s leadership team in Romania and Moldova with more than two decades of experience in accounting, tax and financial leadership. He leads the Accounting & Tax Compliance practice in Romania and Moldova, helping organizations modernize their finance functions and navigate an increasingly evolving regulatory environment. Recognized for his experience in finance function transformation, team development and the use of technology to drive performance, Alexandru works with entrepreneurs and international companies to build more agile and future-ready organizations. An ACCA, CECCAR and CCF member, Alexandru is actively involved in promoting professional excellence and innovation in the accounting and finance field. Ramona Jurubiță, Country Managing Partner, KPMG in Romania and Moldova , said: “This moment is, above all, the result of the trust placed in us by our clients and partners, as well as the extraordinary contribution of our colleagues, to whom I would like to express my gratitude. At the same time, it is marked both by the promotion of outstanding professionals into leadership roles and by the strengthening of our presence within KPMG’s leadership structures across Central and Eastern Europe. These appointments reflect the professionalism and continuous development of the KPMG team in Romania and Moldova, as well as our commitment to developing leaders who contribute to KPMG’s success at both local and regional levels. I am confident that Raluca, Alexandru, Mădălina and René will continue to create value for our clients, teams and organization in their new roles.” Post Views: 12,973 Tags KPMG Romania Latest articles Energy Radu Vasile, Eximprod Engineering: “Renewable energy producers should choose an EPC contractor with in-house design capabilities to speed up projects” Grid connection infrastructure, procurement of high-voltage equipment and project design are among the main... https://www.thetablet.co.uk/news/news-br.text: News Briefing: Church in the World Patrick Hudson , Bess Twiston Davies , Sarah Mac Donald , Marko Phiri , Natalie K. Watson , Brian Fraga 10 October 2026, The Tablet Prev Next A Czech court granted full legal rehabilitation to Cardinal Stepan Trochta (1905-74), a leading member of the underground church during the Communist regime. Wikimedia Commons The Syriac Catholic Patriarch of Antioch Ignatius Youseff III Younan said a meeting called by bishops of the Church last week was “unlawful”. In a statement on 28 September, Patriarch Younan said the motu proprio Mutua Concordia issued by Pope Leo in August only permits a senior bishop of an Eastern Catholic Church to call a synod if the patriarch has failed to do so, but he maintained he had fulfilled this obligation on 2 September by inviting the bishops to a synod on 17-20 November. Younan asked the bishops “to participate in a spirit of communion and fraternal love in the synod” in November and insisted he “remains open-hearted and ready for any opinion, dialogue, frank discussion and fraternal meeting at any time, for the good of the Church and the salvation of souls , whether during, before, or after the synod meeting”. Ethiopia ’s bishops appealed for peace and reconciliation in response to worsening violence that threatens to return the country to civil war , warning that conflict harms the most vulnerable. In a pastoral letter the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Ethiopia (CBCE) said the Church “grieves deeply” over the armed conflict in Tigray, Afar, Amhara, Oromia and other regions. The fighting broke out after Tigrayan rebels formed a new coalition – the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival – aimed at overthrowing the government in Addis Ababa. It is the most serious challenge yet to the 2022 Pretoria Agreement that ended the 2020-22 war in Tigray which caused up to 600,000 deaths. In their statement, the bishops appealed to all sides “to regard the life of others as we regard our own life and the suffering of others as our own suffering, because the peace of our beloved nation, Ethiopia, is a responsibility shared by all of us”. They called for them to settle the dispute through dialogue and for a cessation of the conflict. Echoing Pope Leo, they emphasised that violence causes the greatest suffering to the most vulnerable , particularly children, women, the elderly and the sick. A multi-vehicle road crash in Kenya killed at least 17 people including pilgrims travelling to a prayer site. Following the accident at Salama on the Nairobi-Mombasa highway in the early hours of 3 October, Archbishop Martin Kivuva Musonde of Mombasa confirmed that the dead came from a parish in his diocese. They were travelling to mark Kenya’s National Prayer Day at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Rosary in Nakuru County. “Let us pray for the repose of their souls as we pray for their families, St Mathias Mulumba Parish and the archdiocese as a whole, so that we may find solace and consolation in the Lord,” the archbishop said in a statement. The Inter-Regional Meeting of the Bishops of Southern Africa (IMBISA) called for an end to violence in Mozambique ’s Cabo Delgado province where a jihadist campaign has left thousands dead. Government forces have been accused of failing to protect civilians from al-Shabaab insurgents, who have imposed sharia law in parts of the region and caused mass displacement of the local population. IMBISA vice president Archbishop José Manuel Imbamba of Saurímo, in Angola, told reporters last week that the region’s situation was worsening with more families abandoning their homes. According to aid agencies, close to 7,000 people have died and another 1.5 million have been displaced since 2017 when the rebels launched their assault on local communities . IMBISA leaders said they visited the Cabo Delgado region to assess the situation and express solidarity with the local bishop. Archbishop Imbamba said peace efforts remain urgent to address “extreme violence”. Aid agencies have warned that the trauma of the war means victims need counselling as well as humanitarian support . Caritas Sierra Leone said an extradition dispute between the government and the European Union could threaten humanitarian work. The EU reportedly suspended critical aid funding worth US$20 million to pressure Sierra Leone authorities to cooperate with the extradition of a suspected drug trafficker of European origin who fled there. Caritas said the cuts had an immediate effect on its aid programmes . “I appeal to our government to address this matter urgently, transparently and through lawful cooperation,” said Fr Peter Konteh, executive director of Caritas. “Any allegation of protection for a convicted trafficker must be properly investigated. The interests of our people must come before personal relationships or political convenience.” The Commission of European Union Bishops’ Conferences (Comece) expressed concern over an opinion issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in a case concerning the erasure of baptismal registers. The case concerns the integrity of Catholic baptismal registers in the face of attempts to force the deletion of records under EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) laws. It follows a case in Belgium where a man who renounced his Catholic faith sued to have his baptismal record erased. While a civil court ordered the erasure, the Church appealed the decision to the ECJ . According to Comece, the non-binding opinion of the ECJ’s advocate general has left room for a role for the national courts. Comece highlighted several reasons why erasing names from baptismal registries would cause systemic harm including to Church autonomy. These include the argument that sacrament of baptism and its effect cannot be equated with “membership” applicable to associations under civil law and that baptismal registries are considered “vital civil evidence” and as such are historically and legally significant outside of religion. “In many EU countries, they serve as official documentation relied upon by secular states for establishing legal rights, inheritance, citizenship, pensions and civil property claims,” Comece said. Cardinal Matteo Zuppi visited Ukrainian prisoners of war during three days in Russia as part of his mission as the Pope’s humanitarian envoy. During his visit to Russia on 28-30 September, the cardinal met President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ashokov, as well as Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights, Yana Lantratova, and Commissioner for Children’s Rights, Maria Lvova-Belova, discussing the treatment of military and civilian prisoners and the repatriation of children displaced by the war in Ukraine. “We need to strengthen and speed up the checks needed to ensure that families can be reunited,” Zuppi said. His visit to prisoners of war mirrored his meeting with Russian prisoners during a visit to Ukraine in July. A Czech court granted full legal rehabilitation to Cardinal Stepan Trochta (1905-74), a leading member of the Czech underground church. The court in Litoměřice confirmed that Trochta, who was Bishop of Litoměřice from 1947 until his death, had been illegally deprived of his freedom from 19 July 1950 to 16 January 1953. Trochta, a Salesian, had already been persecuted during the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia . Following his release from Dachau, Pope Pius XII made him Bishop of Litoměřice. He and other bishops opposed the Communist regime and Trochta spent seven years in prison following a show trial. Even after his release, he was not allowed to exercise his episcopal office and at times had to work as a labourer. He returned to episcopal duties after the Prague Spring in 1968 and was created a cardinal in pectore by Pope Paul VI. He was subject to hours of interrogation by state security officials the day before he died from a stroke. Czech Catholics regard Trochta as a martyr, though efforts to open a cause for his canonisation have faltered. Cardinal Christoph Schönborn criticised the ban on headscarves for girls under 14 in Austrian schools. “Neither I nor the teachers can decide what is coercion and what is freedom ,” he told Heute . “What about the seven-year-old who makes their first holy communion? Or the Jewish boy who wears a kippa? How much freedom is there – or to what extent is religion a part of family life that is taken for granted?” Schönborn, the former Archbishop of Vienna, said the state should interfere as little as possible, and religion should not be turned into an instrument of political power. “If, as in France, all religious symbols are forbidden , then I as a religious representative wouldn’t even be permitted to wear a pectoral cross when visiting a school,” he continued, emphasising that different faith communities should value each other and learn tolerance: “We shouldn’t pretend that Christians have always been world champions of tolerance.” The Archbishop of Madrid Cardinal José Cobo called Spain ’s housing crisis a “problem that is extremely radical in the public life of our society” on the eve of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s announcement of a snap election. Speaking last week, Cardinal Cobo said “major agreements and major pacts” were necessary to deal with the issue “in financial, political and social terms”. He insisted that “that major problems of our society like housing are not new. What the Church doesn’t want to do right now is get involved in existing polarisation.” He was referring to controversy over the cost of rental housing prompted by the eviction last month of an 87-year-old woman named Mari Carmen from the home she had lived in for 71 years. She paid €500 per month in rent, an amount established according to a rental contract signed by her father in 1956. When an investment firm acquired the building including her flat, it claimed it could not comply with ancient legal mechanisms that had once protected rental increases in Spain. It demanded Mari Carmen pay €2,650 a month, a sum exceeding her pension of €1,350. An anonymous donor offered to pay the difference but the investment firm refused and evicted Mari Carmen despite neighbours and young people blocking the access of eviction officers to her flat. She was evicted on a stretcher on the fourth attempt to remove her and taken to hospital, where she died on 7 October. In response to the public outcry, Sánchez tried to pass emergency legislation on housing rentals including a ban on evictions and limits on the amount of property purchasing power accorded to “vulture” investment funds. Right-wing parties and the Catalan nationalist party Junts blocked the legislation in the Spanish Congress , where the prime minister’s PSOE (Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party) has a minority, leading him to call an election on Monday. Nearly 200 male and female prisoners from Spanish jails completed the Camino de Santiago. Their pilgrimage was the fifth organised by the Penitentiary Pastoral Ministry of the Spanish Bishops’ Conference. The Archbishop of Pamplona and Bishop of Tudela, Florencio Roselló, who is the lead for prison ministry in the Spanish Bishops’ Conference, joined the pilgrimage with 73 prison officers and 83 volunteers. He invited the pilgrims to “raise their eyes” above walls and bars to discover a horizon peopled by family and friends , where freedom and opportunities exist. In a homily at the closing Mass, which Roselló concelebrated alongside the Archbishop of Santiago de Compostela, he echoed a phrase Pope Leo XIV addressed to prisoners during his visit in June to Spain: “God loves you as you are but dreams of a better you .” Many of the pilgrims wore T-shirts emblazoned with that phrase, noted Roselló. He invited them to believe the words and recognise the promise of a future in them. Erika, a prisoner who took part in the pilgrimage, thanked the chaplains and volunteers for being approachable. With them she had found a place where she had felt heard without being judged , she said. Pope Leo XIV said relations between Lutherans and Catholics have “matured both spiritually and theologically over the decades”. He was addressing leaders of the Lutheran World Federation (LWF) at an audience in the Vatican on 1 October. Bishop Henrik Stubkjær, the president of the LWF, thanked Pope Leo for his repeated calls for “disarmament, the rejection of weapons and the need for dialogue”, and for the concerns he expressed in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas regarding the future of artificial intelligence . “The LWF understands itself as a movement within the one ecumenical movement for the sake of the one church catholic,” said Stubkjær. He referred to the Joint Lutheran-Catholic Commemoration of the five-hundredth anniversary of the Reformation in 2016, signed “exactly 10 years ago this month”. The Pope and the Lutherans voiced hopes for a joint commemoration of the five-hundredth anniversary of the Augsburg Confession in June 2030. Co-written by Martin Luther, this statement chiefly listing the similarities and differences between Catholics and Lutherans. It was presented to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V by German rulers on 25 June 1530. “Renewed communion in the apostolic faith, in the sacraments and in the ministries, is the goal of our ecumenical journey of grace, which we walk together guided by the gospel,” Pope Leo said. “On our journey from conflict to communion there are special moments. The year 2030 [….] can become one such shared moment : a profound ecumenical experience that can give new energy and joy to the steps we will take towards full visible unity.” Pope Leo appointed Cardinal Mauro Gambetti OFM Conv, the 60-year-old archpriest of St Peter’s, as Archbishop of Chieti-Vasto in central Italy , succeeding Archbishop Bruno Forte who retired aged 77. Pope Francis made Gambetti a cardinal in November 2020, when he was Custos General of the General Custody of the Sacred Convent of Saint Francis in Assisi, and the following February appointed him archpriest and president of the Fabric of St Peter, which cares for the basilica . Pope Leo did not immediately name his successor in the post. Two Roman tribunals reached “moral certainty” that the late Argentine priest Carlos Miguel Buela was guilty of “acts constituting an offence against the sixth commandment, committed with violence against several people”. The Special Penal Tribunal of the First Instance and the Appeals Tribunal announced the decision in statement on 29 September signed by Sr Simona Brambilla, prefect of the Dicastery for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life, and by the two pontifical delegates assigned to the Institutes of the Incarnate Word and the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará – the male and female branches of the religious order founded by Buela in the 1980s. The statement said the judgment would help “to ensure that members of both institutes are duly informed and to support the process of re-examining the charism and reviewing, renewing and purifying the spirituality, formation and apostolate proper to each institute”. A 70-year-old bishop and vicar general was removed from office in Argentina following a canonical trial. Bishop Ricardo Seirutti was an auxiliary of the Archdiocese of Cordoba. According to a statement dated 2 October, Seirutti was removed from office following an open trial due to “ complaints of inappropriate conduct for a bishop ” made by two adults. The Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith had ordered a judicial trial which was held in the inter-diocesan tribunal of Buenos Aires, said the statement. He is banned from receiving new appointments and from administering the Sacrament of Reconciliation for a five-year period, but is allowed to celebrate Mass and other sacraments.
